patient.name: Dorothy Pemberton
patient.complaint: Found on the floor at home; admitted after a long lie, now bedbound
background: Left-sided stroke 2 years ago, walks with a frame
Lives alone in Bromley with carers twice daily

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate classification?' or 'most likely diagnosis' for an immobile patient: the stage is decided by the deepest tissue you can see.

points: Dorothy, 86, lay on her kitchen floor **overnight**.
On the ward she barely moves in bed.
She is thin, incontinent of urine and eats little.
Day 2: a nurse finds **redness over her sacrum**.

steps.lead: Dorothy's long lie and immobility put pressure on her sacrum for hours; she adds **malnutrition** and **incontinence** to the risk list.
On admission Dorothy should have had a **Waterlow score** to flag her risk before any damage appeared.

visual.title: Dorothy's Waterlow score
visual.label: Dorothy 24
visual.caption: Age, thin build, incontinence, poor appetite, immobility and neurology push her into **very high risk**.

steps.lead: Dorothy's sacrum is the classic site. Heels, greater trochanters and elbows are the other bony prominences to check.

steps.q: Dorothy's sacral skin is red, intact and does not blanch when pressed. Which stage?
steps.r: **Non-blanching erythema with intact skin** is stage 1. Any skin loss makes it stage 2 or deeper.

steps.lead: Staging is by depth. Dorothy starts at **stage 1**; a week later she has a full-thickness ulcer into fat, **stage 3**.

steps.title: Staging a pressure ulcer
nodes: Partial thickness: blister, shallow red bed → Stage 2
Full thickness into subcutaneous fat → Stage 3
Muscle, tendon or bone exposed → Stage 4
steps.caption: Ask: is the skin broken? How deep is the deepest point?

steps.text: A wound covered in **black eschar** cannot be staged: call it **ungradable**, not stage 4. You cannot see the depth until it is debrided.

points: Day 10: the sacral ulcer is 4 cm, through to fat.
Surrounding skin now **hot, red and spreading**.
Dorothy is more confused and feverish.

steps.lead: Dorothy's ulcer is now infected. Watch for osteomyelitis and **sepsis**, and treat spreading necrosis as a possible **necrotising soft tissue infection**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?': clinical examination for diagnosis and staging, a wound swab (after saline cleaning) if infected, MRI for suspected osteomyelitis.

steps.q: What confirms and stages Dorothy's pressure ulcer?
steps.r: **Clinical examination** is the gold standard. There is no specific lab marker.

steps.lead: Dorothy's ulcer is diagnosed and staged at the **bedside** by looking at it and measuring it.

steps.title: Dorothy's bloods on day 10
steps.text: Raised inflammatory markers mean infection. Low albumin reflects malnutrition and illness, which slow healing.

steps.lead: Infection is suspected, so the nurse **cleans Dorothy's ulcer with sterile saline first**, then takes a wound swab.

steps.text: A swab from an unclean wound grows skin and faecal **colonisers**. Clean with saline first, and swab only when infection is clinically suspected.

steps.lead: If Dorothy's ulcer reached bone (stage 4) with suspected **osteomyelitis** or abscess, **MRI** would be the next test.

steps.text: Exam ladder: diagnose = **clinical examination**; infected = **swab after saline**; stage 4 with bone involvement = **MRI**.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': pressure relief for every stage, hydrocolloid for uninfected stage 2, debridement for stage 3, flucloxacillin if infected, surgery for stage 4.

steps.q: What is the first thing to do for every pressure ulcer, whatever the stage?
steps.r: **Pressure relief** is first-line at every stage: without it nothing heals.

steps.lead: Dorothy gets an air mattress, **2 to 4 hourly turns** and a cushion; an uninfected stage 2 ulcer would get a **hydrocolloid** dressing.
Dorothy's stage 3 ulcer needs **debridement** of the slough plus moist dressings; it is infected, so she starts **flucloxacillin**.
Had Dorothy's ulcer reached bone (stage 4), she would need **surgical debridement** and possibly a reconstructive flap.

visual.title: Dorothy's sacral ulcer with treatment
visual.caption: Antibiotics settle the infection fast; healing takes weeks of pressure relief and nutrition.

steps.lead: Dorothy's care follows **NICE CG179**: risk assessment with Waterlow, repositioning, pressure-relieving surfaces, nutrition and wound care.

steps.text: Treat the **cause** too: dietitian review for Dorothy's low albumin and continence care to stop maceration.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why pressure causes necrosis (capillary closing pressure), why shear and friction worsen it, and why malnutrition and incontinence raise risk.

steps.lead: Lying on the floor all night, Dorothy's weight squeezed her sacral skin above **capillary closing pressure**, so the tissue became ischaemic and died.

steps.title: From pressure to ulcer
nodes: Body weight over a bony prominence

visual.title: Pressure under Dorothy's sacrum on the floor
visual.label: About 90 mmHg
visual.caption: Above roughly **32 mmHg** capillaries close. Hours like this on a hard floor cause necrosis.

steps.text: Why repositioning every few hours matters: it lets the capillaries refill.

steps.lead: Each time Dorothy slides down the bed, **shear** and friction tear the small vessels further.

steps.q: Why does Dorothy's low albumin and poor diet slow healing?
steps.r: **Malnutrition impairs collagen synthesis** and wound healing. Maceration comes from incontinence.

steps.lead: Dorothy has both: poor nutrition stops repair, and urine **macerates** her skin, so it breaks down faster and heals slower.
Dorothy went from reversible **stage 1** to stage 3: the stage tracks how deep the damage goes, so it sets how intense treatment must be.

mcq.q: What defines a stage 1 pressure ulcer?
What defines a stage 4 pressure ulcer?
mcq.r: Stage 4 = full-thickness loss with **exposed muscle, tendon or bone**.

mcq.q: When is a pressure ulcer called ungradable?
o: Covered by eschar so depth is unknown
mcq.r: **Eschar** hides the depth, so it cannot be staged.

mcq.q: Which score assesses pressure ulcer risk?
What is the gold standard for diagnosing a pressure ulcer?
mcq.r: **Clinical examination**; there is no specific lab marker.

mcq.q: What must you do before a wound swab?
mcq.r: **Clean with sterile saline** first to avoid swabbing colonisers.

mcq.q: Which test for suspected osteomyelitis under a stage 4 ulcer?
mcq.r: **MRI** for osteomyelitis, abscess or deep infection.

mcq.q: Which dressing for a non-infected stage 2 pressure ulcer?
What is first-line antibiotic for an infected pressure ulcer?
Why does sustained pressure cause necrosis?
mcq.r: Pressure above **capillary closing pressure** causes local ischaemia.

prompts.q: What is a pressure ulcer and who is at risk?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem will tell you the patient cannot move.

points.p: Localised skin/tissue damage from prolonged pressure over a bony prominence
points.why: Pressure reduces blood flow and causes necrosis.

points.p: Bedbound or immobile
points.why: The key risk factor in almost every stem.

points.p: Spinal cord injury
Malnutrition
Incontinence

prompts.q: Where do pressure ulcers occur and how do they present?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the bony prominences.

points.p: Sacrum
points.why: A sacral ulcer suggests an immobile patient.

points.p: Heels
Greater trochanter and elbows
Pain over the pressure area; ulcer over a bony prominence; no specific lab marker

prompts.q: Describe each pressure ulcer stage, including ungradable.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: classification SBAs are common; go by the deepest tissue.

points.p: Stage 1: non-blanching erythema, intact skin
Stage 2: partial thickness (epidermis + dermis), blister or shallow red bed
Stage 3: full thickness into subcutaneous tissue
points.why: Bone, tendon and muscle not exposed.

points.p: Stage 4: exposed muscle, tendon or bone
Ungradable: covered by eschar, depth unknown

prompts.q: What complications can a pressure ulcer cause, and what is the emergency to consider?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: deep ulcers reach bone.

points.p: Infection (cellulitis)
Osteomyelitis
Sepsis
Chronic non-healing ulcer
points.why: If the cause is not removed.

points.p: Necrotising soft tissue infection if spreading necrosis and systemic illness

prompts.q: How do you assess pressure ulcer risk?

points.p: Waterlow score
Used in at-risk patients, e.g. on admission

prompts.q: How is a pressure ulcer investigated, from diagnosis to complications?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: clinical first, then swab, then MRI.

points.p: Clinical examination is the gold standard
Infection suspected: wound swab
points.why: Only if infection is clinically suspected.

points.p: Clean with sterile saline before swabbing
Stage 4 with osteomyelitis or abscess: MRI
points.why: MRI shows bone marrow oedema early.

prompts.q: What is the first-line management of a pressure ulcer?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: relieve the pressure first, always.

points.p: Regular repositioning
Pressure-relieving devices or mattress, cushions
Hydrocolloid dressing for non-infected stage 2 (with foam)

prompts.q: How do you manage a stage 3, infected or stage 4 pressure ulcer?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: escalate by depth and infection.

points.p: Stage 3: debridement of necrotic tissue plus moist dressings
Infected: flucloxacillin first-line
Penicillin allergy: clarithromycin (co-amoxiclav also used)
Stage 4: surgical debridement, may need reconstruction

prompts.q: Why does pressure cause necrosis, and why do shear and friction make it worse?

points.p: Sustained pressure exceeds capillary closing pressure
points.why: Flow stops in the compressed tissue.

points.p: Local ischaemia progresses to necrosis and ulceration
Shear and friction (sliding down the bed) disrupt the microvasculature
points.why: Why patients are lifted, not dragged.

prompts.q: Why do malnutrition and incontinence raise risk, and why does stage guide treatment?

points.p: Malnutrition impairs collagen synthesis and wound healing
Incontinence causes skin maceration
Stage reflects depth: reversible stage 1 to exposed deep structures in stage 4

glossary.pressure ulcer: Skin and tissue damage from prolonged pressure over a bony prominence.
glossary.pressure sore: Another name for a pressure ulcer or bedsore.
glossary.bony prominence: An area where bone lies close under the skin, such as the sacrum or heel.
glossary.sacrum: The triangular bone at the base of the spine, the commonest pressure ulcer site.
glossary.greater trochanter: The bony bump on the outer upper thigh at the hip.
glossary.non-blanching erythema: Redness that does not fade when pressed; the sign of stage 1 damage.
glossary.blanch: To turn pale when pressed, as normal skin does.
glossary.partial thickness: Skin loss through the epidermis and part of the dermis only.
glossary.full thickness: Skin loss through the whole dermis into the tissue beneath.
glossary.epidermis: The outer layer of the skin.
glossary.dermis: The layer of skin beneath the epidermis, containing vessels and collagen.
glossary.subcutaneous tissue: The fatty layer beneath the dermis.
glossary.eschar: Thick, dry, black dead tissue covering a wound.
glossary.slough: Soft, yellow dead tissue in a wound bed.
glossary.ungradable: A pressure ulcer whose depth cannot be judged because eschar or slough covers it.
glossary.Waterlow score: A risk assessment score for developing pressure ulcers; higher means greater risk.
glossary.Waterlow: Pressure ulcer risk score: 10 at risk, 15 high risk, 20 very high risk.
glossary.repositioning: Regularly changing a patient's position to relieve pressure.
glossary.hydrocolloid: A moist, gel-forming dressing used for shallow uninfected wounds.
glossary.foam dressing: An absorbent padded dressing that cushions and manages exudate.
glossary.debridement: Removal of dead or infected tissue from a wound.
glossary.wound swab: A sample from a wound sent to find the infecting organism.
glossary.maceration: Softening and breakdown of skin kept wet for too long.
glossary.shear: Force when skin stays still while deeper tissue slides, tearing small vessels.
glossary.friction: Rubbing of skin against a surface, damaging the outer layers.
glossary.capillary closing pressure: The external pressure that collapses capillaries and stops blood flow (about 32 mmHg).
glossary.ischaemia: Inadequate blood supply to a tissue.
glossary.flucloxacillin: Narrow-spectrum penicillin active against Staphylococcus aureus.
glossary.clarithromycin: Macrolide antibiotic used when a patient is allergic to penicillin.
glossary.co-amoxiclav: Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid, a broad-spectrum penicillin.
glossary.necrotising soft tissue infection: Rapidly spreading infection destroying skin, fat and fascia; a surgical emergency.
glossary.NICE CG179: The NICE guideline on preventing and managing pressure ulcers.
glossary.albumin: Main blood protein; low levels suggest malnutrition or illness.
glossary.reconstructive surgery: Surgery, such as a flap, to close a large tissue defect.

technique.stem: An 81 year old woman has been bedbound for 3 weeks after a hip fracture. A nurse finds an ulcer over her sacrum. It extends through the full thickness of the skin into the subcutaneous fat. No muscle, tendon or bone is visible and there is no eschar. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 132/76 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate classification of this pressure ulcer?

steps.x: A staging question: find the deepest tissue described.

clues: full thickness of the skin into the subcutaneous fat
No muscle, tendon or bone is visible
steps.x: Full thickness into fat, no deep structures, depth visible.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Stage 2 is partial thickness, sparing fat.
Stage 4 needs exposed muscle, tendon or bone.
Ungradable needs eschar hiding the depth.

steps.x: **C. Stage 3.** Into fat = 3; bone, muscle or tendon = 4.

technique.stem: A 79 year old man with Parkinson's disease is admitted with pneumonia and has been immobile for 5 days. There is a 2 cm shallow open area over his right heel with a red wound bed. There is no surrounding redness, warmth or discharge. His temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and BP 126/74 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate way to confirm and stage this pressure ulcer?

steps.x: How to confirm and stage a pressure ulcer.

clues: shallow open area over his right heel
no surrounding redness, warmth or discharge

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: No specific lab marker; CRP does not stage.
MRI is for stage 4 with suspected osteomyelitis.
Biopsy is for suspected malignancy, not routine.
Swab only when infection is suspected.

technique.stem: An 88 year old woman with advanced dementia lives in a nursing home and is bedbound. Her Waterlow score is 22. There is non-blanching redness over her sacrum with intact skin. There is no warmth or discharge. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 124/70 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

clues: non-blanching redness over her sacrum with intact skin
steps.x: Very high risk; stage 1; not infected.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pressure relief**: repositioning and a pressure-relieving mattress.

elim: Steroids thin skin and do not relieve pressure.

technique.stem: An 84 year old man has a stage 3 sacral pressure ulcer that has failed to heal despite repositioning and dressings for 6 weeks. He has lost 8 kg in 3 months and eats little. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 118/68 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which his nutrition delays healing?
o: Impaired collagen synthesis and wound healing

steps.x: Mechanism linking malnutrition to poor healing.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Not the mechanism of poor healing.
Malnutrition does not raise capillary closing pressure.
Venous stasis is a venous ulcer mechanism.

steps.x: **B.** No protein, no collagen, no healing.

practice.stem: An 83 year old woman has been confined to bed for 4 days after a stroke. Over her left heel there is an area of red skin that does not blanch when pressed. The skin is intact with no blister. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 76 bpm and BP 146/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate classification of this pressure ulcer?
practice.e: Non-blanching erythema with intact skin is stage 1. Any blister or skin loss is at least stage 2.

clues: The skin is intact with no blister

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Stage 2 needs partial skin loss or a blister.
Stage 4 exposes muscle, tendon or bone.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man with paraplegia from a spinal cord injury has a deep ulcer over his right ischial tuberosity. The base shows exposed bone and tendon. His temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 86 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate classification of this pressure ulcer?
practice.e: Full-thickness loss with exposed bone, tendon or muscle is stage 4.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: The base is visible, so it can be staged.

practice.stem: A 90 year old woman in a nursing home is bedbound with dementia. Over her sacrum there is a 5 cm area covered by thick, dry, black, leathery tissue. The depth of the wound cannot be seen. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 120/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate classification of this pressure ulcer?
practice.e: An ulcer covered by eschar cannot have its depth assessed, so it is ungradable until debrided.

steps.x: Staging: can you see the base?

clues: depth of the wound cannot be seen

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: No bone or tendon can be seen; do not assume stage 4.

practice.stem: A 77 year old man has been in hospital for 10 days after a hip replacement and moves little in bed. There is a shallow open wound over his sacrum with a red-pink wound bed and a ruptured blister. Subcutaneous fat is not visible. His temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and BP 134/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate classification of this pressure ulcer?
practice.e: Partial-thickness skin loss with a shallow red bed or blister, sparing fat, is stage 2.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

steps.x: **B. Stage 2.** Blister or shallow red bed = 2.

practice.stem: An 82 year old woman with Parkinson's disease has been bedbound for a month with a urinary catheter. She has a painful 3 cm ulcer over her sacrum. Foot pulses are palpable and there is no leg swelling. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 128/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A sacral ulcer over a bony prominence in a bedbound patient is a pressure ulcer. Arterial and venous ulcers affect the leg and foot.

steps.x: Ulcer diagnosis: where is it and who is the patient?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Arterial ulcers are distal on the foot with absent pulses.
No rolled edge or long history to suggest malignancy.
Pyoderma has a violaceous undermined edge, often with IBD.
Venous ulcers are in the gaiter area.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man with multiple sclerosis has a stage 4 sacral pressure ulcer with exposed bone. He has new deep sacral pain and fever for a week. His temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 124/70 mmHg.
practice.e: A stage 4 ulcer over exposed bone with deep pain, fever and a high ESR suggests osteomyelitis, confirmed with MRI.

steps.x: Complication of a deep pressure ulcer.

clues: stage 4 sacral pressure ulcer with exposed bone
new deep sacral pain and fever for a week
steps.x: Bone exposed, deep pain, raised ESR.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Cellulitis is spreading skin redness, not deep bone pain.
Would be rapidly spreading with severe systemic illness.
A pilonidal abscess is in the natal cleft, not from a pressure ulcer.

practice.stem: An 85 year old woman has a stage 3 sacral pressure ulcer. Over 2 days the surrounding skin has become hot, red and swollen with purulent discharge. Her temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 130/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
o: Wound swab after cleaning with saline
practice.e: With suspected infection, take a wound swab after cleaning with sterile saline. MRI is for suspected osteomyelitis in stage 4.

steps.x: Initial investigation for an infected pressure ulcer.

clues: hot, red and swollen with purulent discharge

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Cultures may help in sepsis but do not sample the wound.
MRI is for stage 4 with suspected osteomyelitis.
X-ray is insensitive and not first-line.

practice.stem: A 66 year old man with tetraplegia has a stage 4 sacral pressure ulcer with exposed bone. He has had a fever and worsening sacral pain for 10 days. His temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 116/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
practice.e: A stage 4 ulcer with suspected osteomyelitis or abscess needs MRI. A swab does not show bone infection.

steps.x: Investigation of a complicated stage 4 ulcer.

clues: stage 4 sacral pressure ulcer with exposed bone
fever and worsening sacral pain for 10 days

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: X-ray changes lag behind by weeks.
Grows surface organisms, not bone infection.

practice.stem: An 80 year old woman recovering from pneumonia has a shallow open ulcer over her sacrum with a red wound bed. There is no surrounding redness, warmth or discharge. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 128/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: A non-infected stage 2 ulcer needs pressure relief and a hydrocolloid (or foam) dressing. Antibiotics are only for infection.

clues: no surrounding redness, warmth or discharge

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

practice.stem: A 78 year old man has an infected stage 3 pressure ulcer on his sacrum with spreading redness. A swab has been taken. He had anaphylaxis to penicillin in the past. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 132/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
practice.e: Flucloxacillin is first-line for an infected pressure ulcer, but with penicillin allergy clarithromycin is used.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

practice.stem: A 62 year old woman with spina bifida has a large sacral pressure ulcer with exposed bone and muscle. Repositioning, dressings and antibiotics have not helped. MRI shows no osteomyelitis. Her temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 122/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
practice.e: Stage 4 ulcers need surgical debridement and may need reconstructive surgery, on top of pressure relief.

steps.x: Definitive treatment of a stage 4 ulcer.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Antibiotics alone do not close deep defects.
Needed, but not enough on its own.
Will not heal a stage 4 ulcer.

practice.stem: An 87 year old man lay on a hard floor for 14 hours after a fall. Two days later there is non-blanching redness over his sacrum and both heels. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 136/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of this tissue damage?
practice.e: Sustained pressure over bony prominences exceeds capillary closing pressure, causing local ischaemia and then necrosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Vasculitis has a purpuric rash, not pressure sites.
